{"id": "2:61/q76", "question": "What wilderness narrative does Biqāʿī quote from the Torah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q76/p1", "position": "Biqāʿī quotes a continuous departure and wilderness account", "reasons": "BIQAI-FULL: The Qur'anic sequence of Israel's stories is not chronological; the author says the Torah's important correspondences explain its arrangement. BIQAI-FULL: The author says he consulted a current ninth-century Jewish copy of the Torah's fourth book, in an Arabic translation marked with reading times, and compared it with the meaning alongside a Jewish reader. BIQAI-FULL: The Torah itinerary places Israel's departure from Rameses, also called Ain Shams in a variant, on the fifteenth of Nisan after Passover, with a variant dating it one day after Passover; Egyptians were burying their firstborn as Israel left armed. BIQAI-FULL: The cited Torah says Egypt was occupied with burying its slain firstborn and that the Lord had taken vengeance on the Egyptians' gods as Israel departed. BIQAI-FULL: The Torah itinerary continues along the Red Sea coast, with variant names for the sea and several wilderness encampments through Rithmah. BIQAI-FULL: At Rephidim there was no drinking water; the itinerary gives a variant name for the station. BIQAI-FULL (موسى): Moses commands Israel to remember its liberation from Egyptian slavery through the annual festival of unleavened bread, observed for seven days, and to teach its meaning to their children. BIQAI-FULL (موسى): Moses says the observance is a sign and memorial because God brought Israel out with a mighty hand, and it should be kept year after year. BIQAI-FULL (موسى): The Torah passage commands consecrating every firstborn male animal to God, redeeming it with a lamb or slaughtering it, and redeeming each firstborn son. BIQAI-FULL (موسى): When a child asks why the rite is performed, the parent is to recount that God brought Israel out of bondage and killed Egypt's firstborn, explaining the sacrifice and redemption of Israel's own firstborn. BIQAI-FULL: The Torah says God avoided the nearby Palestine road lest Israel see battle and flee back to Egypt, leading them through the Sea of Reeds wilderness instead. BIQAI-FULL: Israel left armed, while Moses carried Joseph's bones because Joseph had made Israel swear to take them when God remembered and brought them out. BIQAI-FULL: God led them by a cloud pillar in daylightand a fire pillar at night for shade and light, and neither pillar left the people. BIQAI-FULL (الرب): God tells Moses to camp by the sea so Pharaoh will think Israel is lost, then says He will harden Pharaoh's heart, gain glory through him and his army, and teach Egypt that He is Lord. BIQAI-FULL: Pharaoh regrets releasing Israel and pursues with six hundred thousand chosen riders and Egyptian forces; Israel sees the pursuers and panics. BIQAI-FULL (بنو إسرائيل): Israel cries to Moses that Egypt had enough graves and that slavery there would have been better than dying in the wilderness. BIQAI-FULL (موسى): Moses tells the people not to fear: they will witness God's deliverance, will not see the Egyptians again, and God will fight for them while they remain calm. BIQAI-FULL (الرب): God tells Moses to command Israel to move and to lift and strike the sea so the people can cross dry; He will harden Egypt and gain glory through Pharaoh's forces. BIQAI-FULL: The divine pillar moves behind Israel between their camp and Egypt's, with darkness for the Egyptians and light for Israel, preventing approach throughout the night. BIQAI-FULL: The Lord drives the sea back with a hot wind all night, leaving dry ground and walls of water on both sides as Israel crosses. BIQAI-FULL: Egypt's chariots and horses pursue Israel into the sea; at dawn God terrifies the army and disables its chariots, prompting the Egyptians to recognize that the Lord fights for Israel. BIQAI-FULL (الرب): God commands Moses to stretch his hand over the sea; the waters return and drown Pharaoh's forces, with no survivor. BIQAI-FULL: Israel is saved, sees the dead Egyptians and God's great act against them, then fears God and believes and trusts the words of Moses. BIQAI-FULL (موسى وبنو إسرائيل): Moses and Israel sing praise to God as the glorious, eternal warrior who drowned Pharaoh's army; their song describes divine power, rescue, and kingship forever. BIQAI-FULL: The song says surrounding peoples trembled, Israel was led toward the sacred mountain, and God would reign forever; afterward they traveled three days through Shur without water and grumbled at bitter Marah. BIQAI-FULL: God promised evening meat and morning bread so Israel would know that he was their Lord. BIQAI-FULL: Quail covered the camp at evening, and morning dew surrounded it before manna appeared. BIQAI-FULL: The manna appeared as flaky material on the ground, resembling frost. BIQAI-FULL: Moses identified the manna as God's bread and instructed each person to gather one measure according to need for every member of the household. BIQAI-FULL: Although some gathered much and others little, the measured amounts left no surplus for the first or shortage for the latter. BIQAI-FULL: They reached the wilderness of Sin between Elim and Sinai on the fifteenth day of the second month after leaving Egypt. BIQAI-FULL: The Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron, longing for Egypt's meat and bread and accusing them of bringing the people into the wilderness to die of hunger. BIQAI-FULL: God promised bread from heaven and daily gathering as a test of whether Israel would keep his commands. BIQAI-FULL: God commanded a double collection on the sixth day. BIQAI-FULL: Moses and Aaron told the people that God had brought them from Egypt and that they would see his glory the next morning; their complaint had reached him. BIQAI-FULL: Moses said God would give meat in the evening and bread in the morning, and that the people's complaint was against God rather than his messengers. BIQAI-FULL: Aaron brought the congregation near; God's glory appeared in a cloud, and God said he had heard their grumbling. BIQAI-FULL: Some disobeyed Moses by keeping manna overnight; it became wormy and foul, angering Moses. BIQAI-FULL: The measure is glossed as ten jarīb, that is, ten waybas. BIQAI-FULL: Manna was gathered each morning and melted when the sun grew hot. BIQAI-FULL: On the sixth day each person gathered two measures; Moses explained that the next day was a holy Sabbath of rest. BIQAI-FULL: The people were to bake and cook what they needed and keep the remainder cold for the following day. BIQAI-FULL: The saved manna did not spoil; Moses said to eat it on the Sabbath, when none could be gathered in the field, and to gather on the other six days. BIQAI-FULL: Some went out to gather on the seventh day but found none; God rebuked their refusal to accept his commands, and the people rested. BIQAI-FULL: Israel called the food manna; it resembled a coriander seed and tasted like honey. BIQAI-FULL: The fourth book describes manna as coriander-like and white like the mahā, then ground, pounded, cooked into a dish, and tasting like oil-kneaded bread. BIQAI-FULL: Israel ate manna for forty years, until reaching inhabited territory and Canaan. BIQAI-FULL: Al-Biqāʿī cites the Torah's wilderness account: the tabernacle was Israel's qibla, with cloud and night fire signaling when to camp or travel and shading them from the sun. BIQAI-FULL: This segment completes the wilderness narrative: silver horns summoned Israel to the meeting tent and called commanders with one blast; the ark went ahead and the cloud shaded travelers from the sun. BIQAI-FULL: When the people grumbled, fire from God burned the camp's outskirts; Moses prayed and it subsided, so the place was named Burning. BIQAI-FULL: A mixed crowd craved meat and recalled Egypt's fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic; they complained that only manna remained to eat. BIQAI-FULL: Moses said he could not carry the whole nation alone and asked God to kill him rather than let him see further harm. BIQAI-FULL: God appointed seventy elders and shared Moses' spirit with them; a wind brought quail, then a severe plague struck the people while they ate, naming the site Graves of Lust. BIQAI-FULL: After the quail plague, the people left Graves of Lust, reached Hazeroth, and remained there seven days."}]}

{"id": "2:61/q78", "question": "How does the verse relate to the Torah's food account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:61/q78/p1", "position": "Numbers 11 parallels the complaint and quail account", "reasons": "IBNASHUR-FULL: The verse alludes to the Torah's account: after leaving Sinai/Horeb for Paran in year two and traveling toward Hebron, Israelites remembered free fish and produce in Egypt, complained about manna, and wept; God was angered, Moses sought pardon, and God sent quail, which they stored for a month. ASAD-NOTES: Moses asks whether they would trade freedom for the meager comforts of Egyptian captivity; in Sinai they longed for Egypt's comparative security, as Numbers 11 and Moses' next sentence indicate. STUDYQURAN: Numbers 11:4–5 parallels Israel's craving for foods remembered from Egypt, including cucumbers, onions, and garlic. STUDYQURAN: Numbers 11:31–35 says quails were given, but those who craved them were struck down for greed toward God's provision."}]}
{"id": "2:86/q01", "question": "Who are 'those' in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative is identified from the preceding account of Israel or only from its own relative clause.", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q01/p1", "position": "The Jews or Israelites just described as believing part of the Book while violating other covenant commands.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari specifies ransoming captives while killing and expelling protected people; al-Tabrisi points to 2:85. Ibn Abbas is reported by Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan; Ibn Kathir says their selective observance and concealment make their textual testimony unreliable. Abu Hayyan says the demonstrative gathers all their listed traits, as in 2:5; Elmalili adds others like them. Study Quran calls expulsion and ransom hypocrisy, immorality, and a degree of unbelief."}, {"id": "2:86/q01/p2", "position": "They are simply the people God mentions in this verse.", "reasons": "Sa'id ibn Jubayr gives this identification without further specification."}]}
{"id": "2:86/q02", "question": "How do the opening demonstrative and relative clause work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether a second-subject analysis has a required link and whether this specific, past relative clause licenses a conditional fa.", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q02/p1", "position": "أولئك is the subject and الذين, with its relative clause, is the predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas states the subject-predicate construction. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin identify the relative as predicate; al-Samin calls this the correct opening parse."}, {"id": "2:86/q02/p2", "position": "أولئك is the first subject; الذين is a second subject whose predicate is the punishment clause.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports the proposal, and al-Alusi mentions identity of the two referents as its proposed substitute for a linking pronoun but calls it weak. Abu Hayyan and al-Samin object that the nested clause has no link back to أولئك; the analogy هذا زيد منطلق yields separate predicates or a substitute, not an unlinked clause. They add that the specified relative and its past clause lack conditional force to license the fa."}]}
{"id": "2:86/q03", "question": "How is the fa and the punishment clause attached to what precedes?", "turns_on": "Whether the fa coordinates clauses within the relative, marks an implied consequence, or can begin a second predicate through conditional force.", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q03/p1", "position": "The fa clause is coordinated with the relative clause, so it remains within the description of those people.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi makes it part of their relative description. Al-Jishumi prefers this because it follows the text without positing omitted words. Abu Hayyan says two relative-clause complements may have actions in different times; al-Samin agrees. Al-Alusi lists it. Al-Itqan notes the causal fa favors connecting across a permitted stop."}, {"id": "2:86/q03/p2", "position": "The fa introduces a consequence of their purchase, with an implied clause.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi lists this alternative but prefers direct coordination; Ibn Ashur calls the fa consequential because so grave a crime warrants severe punishment and no helper."}, {"id": "2:86/q03/p3", "position": "The punishment clause is a second predicate of أولئك, with fa licensed by the relative's conditional sense.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports the parse. Abu Hayyan objects that conditional force in a relative clause does not pass to the demonstrative it predicates; al-Alusi likewise objects. Al-Samin says fa cannot modify that second predicate."}]}
{"id": "2:86/q04", "question": "What does buying worldly life with the Hereafter mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the exchange is read through outward worldly benefits or through the heart's desires and divine approval.", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q04/p1", "position": "They chose transient worldly gains and surrendered faith, reward, or eternal bliss in the Hereafter; the transaction is figurative.", "reasons": "Muqatil names food gained from the lower classes; al-Tabari names leadership over the weak and ignorant and poor food, and Qatada contrasts little worldly gain with much afterlife gain, also transmitted by Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Durr. Al-Wahidi contrasts small and great gain. Al-Jishumi names abandoning religion and the Messenger for disbelief and adornment, explicitly calling the sale metaphorical. Al-Tabrisi names leadership and lowly benefits. Ibn Atiyya and al-Alusi stress they could have kept the Hereafter; Abu Hayyan says actual trade exchanges goods and price, extended in Arabic to choices, and contrasts transient adornment with lasting bliss. Al-Baghawi glosses exchange; al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, Ibn Kathir and others gloss preference. Al-Nasafi compares the buyer's choice. Al-Wahidi al-Wajiz is not the source here; al-Qurtubi says he discussed this expression earlier without repeating it. Bursevi says their rejection of scripture preserved allies' benefits. Elmalili says they forfeited their future share; Ibn Ashur parallels 2:16's purchase of misguidance with guidance. Kur'an Yolu connects worldly advantage to their punishment and earlier disgrace."}, {"id": "2:86/q04/p2", "position": "In an inward reading, worldly life is the heart's proximate desires, and the Hereafter is what is joined to the Lord's approval.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan attributes this to some interpreters of inner meanings."}]}
{"id": "2:86/q05", "question": "What is the force of the ba in the exchange expression?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q05/p1", "position": "The ba marks what is given up as the price in a purchase.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati says this is the usual Quranic construction and adduces 2:175's exchange of guidance for error and forgiveness for punishment; her note also mentions 9:9."}]}
{"id": "2:86/q06", "question": "What does dunyā mean and derive from?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q06/p1", "position": "It is the near or lower life, from nearness or lowliness, contrasted with the higher or later Hereafter.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan derives it from d-n-w, nearness, and says it is the feminine of adnā. {"id": "2:86/q07", "question": "What forms and uses are recorded for dunyā?", "turns_on": "Dialectal treatment of the original final waw.", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q07/p1", "position": "Dunyā is an adjective and noun; as an adjective its ya replaces an original waw, and its final alif marks feminine form.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan derives it from d-n-w, cites Quranic worldly-life phrases in 10:24 and 18:45, and says omission of its article is confined to poetry, citing a line. {"id": "2:86/q08", "question": "Why pair worldly life with the Hereafter in this wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q08/p1", "position": "The pair has reciprocal ellipsis: worldly life implies a higher life, and the Hereafter implies an immediate life.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i explains each expressed term by its omitted counterpart."}]}

{"id": "2:86/q10", "question": "What does lightening the punishment mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q10/p1", "position": "It means making punishment less heavy, severe, or difficult, whether by reducing it or stopping it.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi relates khiffa to a decrease of weight. {"id": "2:86/q23", "question": "How does this verse connect to the surrounding account and other verses?", "turns_on": "These are complementary links: the local context and verbal parallels elsewhere.", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q23/p1", "position": "It gathers the preceding accusations and explains their worldly disgrace and coming punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari recalls ransoming fellow Jews while killing and expelling others in breach of covenant; Abu Hayyan likens the summary demonstrative to 2:5. {"id": "2:86/q25", "question": "Why is a stop before the punishment clause permitted?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q25/p1", "position": "The following fa favors connection, while the verb begins an independent sentence that permits a stop.", "reasons": "Al-Itqan gives both the causal-resulting fa and independent sentence structure as grounds for a reasoned stop."}]}
{"id": "2:86/q26", "question": "What does khizy in the preceding warning mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:86/q26/p1", "position": "It means humiliation, affliction, or shame.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan cites al-Jawhari's verb khazi and Ibn al-Sikkit's gloss of falling into affliction; he also records forms for a shamed man, group, and woman."}]}
{"id": "2:106/q01", "question": "What does naskh mean in Arabic?", "turns_on": "Whether removal, replacement, transfer, or copying is primary.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q01/p1", "position": "Removal or cancellation, with or without a successor.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Rāzī cite wind erasing traces and 22:52; al-Zajjāj and others cite sun removing shade. Al-Ālūsī describes removal and re-establishment; al-Rāghib treats the usages as related figurative extensions. Al-Rāzī answers the objection that sun and wind are only metaphorical agents by noting their effective role and Arabic usage."}, {"id": "2:106/q01/p2", "position": "Replacement or succession.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj's sun and shade image, Ibn Durayd's generalization, and Muqātil's verse replacement support this sense. {"id": "2:106/q02", "question": "How is ننسخ read and explained?", "turns_on": "The first nūn's vowel and whether Form IV is synonymous, causative, or means finding a thing abrogated.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q02/p1", "position": "The common open-nūn Form I means We abrogate.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī prefers its clarity; the majority reading is listed by Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nashr, and others."}, {"id": "2:106/q02/p2", "position": "Ibn ʿĀmir's ḍamma-nūn Form IV means finding it abrogated.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī rejects an unattested synonym and a causative implying every verse is abrogated; Abū Ḥātim calls the reading erroneous but al-Samīn rebukes him."}, {"id": "2:106/q02/p3", "position": "Ibn ʿĀmir's form is synonymous with Form I or makes a verse abrogated.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī prefers the dialectal synonym; Ibn Khālawayh offers both causative analyses. {"id": "2:106/q04", "question": "What constitutes legal abrogation?", "turns_on": "Whether it is a later proof ending an apparently continuing rule, merely a replacement, or copying.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q04/p1", "position": "A later revealed proof ends a previously binding rule that otherwise would continue.", "reasons": "The Qāḍī, Sunni jurists, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Rāzī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr define it this way; stated expiry or a specification is excluded. {"id": "2:106/q07", "question": "Did abrogation occur in the Qurʾan?", "turns_on": "How to read the conditional verse and how to treat apparent conflicts and examples.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q07/p1", "position": "Yes, some Qurʾanic rulings were superseded.", "reasons": "Majority examples: 2:240/2:234, 8:65/8:66, 58:12/58:13, and qibla change. {"id": "2:106/q08", "question": "Can a rule be abrogated without a replacement?", "turns_on": "Whether 'bring better or like it' requires a successor ruling.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q08/p1", "position": "Yes; lifting a duty may itself be better.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Qurṭubī cite pre-consultation charity or the emigrant women's test; al-Rāzī and al-Ālūsī distinguish a promised benefit from the abrogating rule."}, {"id": "2:106/q08/p2", "position": "No; the verse promises something better or equal.", "reasons": "Some jurists require a substitute; Ibn al-Ḥaṣṣār says extant mutawātir text replaces removed recitation."}]}

{"id": "2:106/q12", "question": "When does an abrogating rule take effect and how is it known?", "turns_on": "Whether notice, performance, or the Prophet's lifetime limits its force.", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q12/p1", "position": "Before notice, the earlier rule still binds; repeal can precede performance.", "reasons": "Leading scholars cite Qubāʾ for notice and Abraham's sacrifice or fifty prayers for repeal before action. {"id": "2:106/q13", "question": "Why must interpreters know abrogation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "2:106/q13/p1", "position": "It is needed to distinguish binding law from superseded law.", "reasons": "ʿAlī warned or expelled an untrained preacher; al-Thaʿlabī and al-Qurṭubī treat naskh as essential to exegesis and lawful/unlawful judgments."}, {"id": "2:106/q13/p2", "position": "Detailed legal-theory debates can obscure this verse's exegesis.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān deliberately leaves the technical disputes to legal theory and criticizes al-Rāzī's expansion."}]}
